Section.Description: Lethal concentration is the estimated concentration of a chemical expected to cause death in a test subject. It is usually expressed as the median lethal concentration (LC50), which is the estimated concentration of a chemical expected to cause death in 50% of the test subjects. There are also other measures such as LC0 (no deaths) and LC100 (all deaths).

Lethal dose values describe the amount of a chemical expected to cause death in test subjects under specified exposure conditions. These values are commonly expressed as dose-based toxicity endpoints such as the median lethal dose (LD50), which represents the estimated dose expected to cause death in 50% of the test subjects. Other endpoints include LD0 (no observed deaths) and LD100 (death in all test subjects).

Effect level values describe the dose or exposure level of a chemical associated with observed biological or toxicological effects in test subjects. These dose-based endpoints include Low Effect Level (LEL), No Effect Level (NEL), Lowest Observed Effect Level (LOEL), No Observed Effect Level (NOEL), Lowest Observed Adverse Effect Level (LOAEL), and No Observed Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL), which represent exposure levels associated with observed or unobserved effects or adverse effects under specified exposure conditions.

Screening levels are health- or environment-based threshold values used to identify chemical concentrations or doses that may warrant additional evaluation or risk assessment. Examples include Ecological Screening Levels (ESLs), Soil Screening Levels (SSLs), Health-Based Screening Levels (HBSLs), and Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) for drinking water.

Reference and risk values are derived toxicity benchmarks used to evaluate potential human health risks associated with chemical exposure. These values are typically developed from experimental toxicity data together with uncertainty or safety factors. Examples include Reference Dose (RfD), Reference Concentration (RfC), Derived No-Effect Level (DNEL), and other health-based guidance or risk assessment values.

Military Exposure Guidelines (MEGs) are established by the Department of Defense (DoD) to evaluate and manage chemical and environmental health risks during deployments. MEGs help determine how chemical exposures in air, water, and soil could impact a service member's health and mission readiness

StringWithMarkup.String: /AQUATIC SPECIES/ Cyprinus carpio was exposed to imazethapyr and imazapic at laboratory and at field conditions. The laboratory experiment was carried out for 7 days and at rice field for 7, 30 and 90 days. Oxidative stress parameters and antioxidant profile were studied as well as metabolic parameters. After 7 days, brain AChE activity increases in laboratory and field, but in muscle, reduction was observed only in laboratory. At the same period, brain and muscle TBARS and liver CAT increase in the laboratory. Metabolic parameters showed changes in both conditions and exposure periods. After 30 days in rice field, brain AChE activity decreases and in muscle it was enhanced. After 90 days in field, only muscle AChE activity was reduced. The disorders in oxidative stress parameters and metabolism remained, indicating mainly a protein catabolism.

Section.Description: This section summarizes the environmental fate/exposure of this chemical, including the natural and artificial sources of the chemical as a pollutant, its environmental fate, biodegradation, abiotic degradation, bioconcentration, etc.

StringWithMarkup.String: Imazethapyr's production may result in its release to the environment through various waste streams; its use as a herbicide will result in its direct release to the environment. If released to air, an estimated vapor pressure of 2.3X10-11 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates imazethapyr will exist solely in the particulate phase in the atmosphere. Particulate-phase imazethapyr will be removed from the atmosphere by wet or dry deposition. If released to soil, imazethapyr is expected to have very high to moderate mobility based upon Koc values of 1.4 to 173. The pKa2 of imazethapyr is 3.9, indicating that this compound will exist almost entirely in anion form in the environment and anions generally do not adsorb more strongly to soils containing organic carbon and clay than their neutral counterparts. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 1.0X10-16 atm-cu m/mole. Although low amounts of imazethapyr were observed to evaporate from dry soil, volatilization is not expected based upon the very low estimated vapor pressure. Photodecomposition of 14C-imazethapyr from Taloka silt loam was 8% for 43 hours. Reported aerobic soil biodegradation half-lives for imazethapyr are 23.5 days to 10.6 months. If released into water, imazethapyr is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon the Koc values. Volatilization from water surfaces is not expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's pKa. An estimated BCF of 3 suggests the potential for bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is low. Reported aqueous photodegradation half-lives for imazethapyr are 4 to 5.1 hours. Hydrolysis is not expected to be an important environmental fate process since this compound lacks functional groups that hydrolyze under environmental conditions. Occupational exposure to imazethapyr may occur through inhalation of spray mists or aerosols and dermal contact with this herbicide during or after its application or at workplaces where imazethapyr is produced. (SRC)

StringWithMarkup.String: AEROBIC: 14C Radio-labeled imazethapyr was incubated for 12 weeks at 28 °C in the dark in two soil types; Drummer silty loam (9% sand, 57% silt, 34% clay, pH 5.7, 5.8% organic carbon) and Cisne silt (14% sand, 74% silt, 12% clay, pH 7.0, 1.3% organic carbon)(1). Imazethapyr was biodegraded 18.2 and 26.8% in Drummer loam when 14C labeled on the carboxyl group and ring structure, respectively(1). Imazethapyr was biodegraded 46.9 and 53.5% in Cisne silt when 14C labeled on the carboxyl group and ring structure, respectively(1). Maury silt loam (8% sand, 67% silt, 25% clay, 2.6% organic matter, pH 6.3) was used in an 8 week study with radio-labeled 14C imazethapyr to determine effects of temperature and moisture on biodegradation(2). 14CO2 evolution from soil incubated at 15 and 30 °C was 1.5 and 4.4% for ring labeled imazethapyr and 2.0 and 5.4% for carboxyl labeled imazethapyr, respectively(2). 14CO2 evolution from ring labeled imazethapyr was 1.1, 3.4, 4.3, 5.4 and 4.6% at 15, 25, 50, 75 and 100% field capacity water content, respectively(2). Biodegradation half-lives of 14C-labeled imazethapyr were 2.6 to 9.0 months for Taloka silt loam (23% sand, 62% silt, 15% clay, 1.7% organic matter, pH 6.3) and 6.4 to 10.6 months for Sharkey silty clay (9% sand, 40% silt, 51% clay, 2.4% organic matter, pH 6.7)(3). Aerobic biodegradation rates were measured in six soils with a range of physico-chemical properties, incubation time was 60 days in the dark at 25 °C and 50% moisture(4). Half-lives were 23.5 to 62.2 days(4). Biodegradation half-lives for imazethapyr in soil are reported as 72.94 to 257.28 days under 33 to 75% field capacity moisture, 10 to 20 °C incubation temperature and 0.1 to 10 ppm initial concentration(5).

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.

StringWithMarkup.String: Imazethapyr had a reported mean Koc of 13.2 (range of 2 to 55) in 101 allophanic and non-allophanic surface soil samples collected throughout New Zealand(1). Imazethapyr had a reported Koc of 19 at pH 7.7 and an increased Koc of 163 as the pH was reduced to 5.4(2). Imazethapyr has a reported Koc range of 75 to 173(3). Koc values for Trani (55.1% sand, 22.0% silt, 22.9% clay, pH 7.5, organic carbon 1.46%) and Andria (69.1% sand, 18% silt, 12.9% clay, pH 7.8, organic carbon 0.62%) soils were 1.4 and 12.9, respectively(4). According to a classification scheme(5), these reported Koc values suggest that imazethapyr is expected to have very high to moderate mobility in soil. In an adsorption study using 2 humic acids, no measurable adsorption of imazethapyr occurred at pH 4.7, while at pH 3.6 and 3.7, the compound did adsorb(6). The pKa2, 3.9, indicates that at the lower pH values, about half of the amount of herbicide would exist in the molecular form and most of the carboxyl groups of humic acids are combined(6); at pH 4.7, the herbicide is mainly in the ionic form and most of the carboxyl groups of humic acids are also ionized(6). Using 10 soils, Kd values ranging from no detectable adsorption (pH 7.5, % organic carbon 0.86-1.39) to 14.74 (pH 4.5, % organic carbon 11.66) were obtained(6).
